title: Comparing an input's value with ===
options: `===` compares references, so two numbers are never equal
`value` is the string "2", and `===` never converts types
`value` stays `undefined` until the form is submitted
`querySelector` returns a copy, so its `value` is empty
explanation: An input's `value` is always a string, so `qty` is "2". Strict equality (`===`) never converts types, and a string is never strictly equal to a number; `Number(qty) === 2` fixes it. Numbers are compared by value, not by reference, the value is available as soon as the user types, and querySelector returns the real element, not a copy.

title: || replaces a valid 0 with the default
options: Use `options.volume && 50`, which keeps any value that is already set
Use `Number(options.volume) || 50`, so 0 is read as a number
Use `options.volume === 0 || 50`, so 0 is checked on its own
Use `options.volume ?? 50`, which falls back on null/undefined only
explanation: `||` falls back whenever the left side is falsy, and 0 is falsy, so a real 0 becomes 50. The nullish coalescing operator `??` falls back only when the left side is null or undefined, so 0 is kept and a missing volume still gives 50. `&&` returns 50 for any truthy volume and undefined when it is missing, `Number(0) || 50` is still 50, and `options.volume === 0 || 50` returns the boolean true.

title: Changing a property of a const object
options: "Bia": const stops reassigning `user`, not changing the object
"Ana": a const object silently ignores property changes
Nothing: line 2 throws a TypeError for changing a constant
Nothing: line 2 is a SyntaxError, so the script never runs
explanation: `const` makes the binding constant: `user` can never point to another value, so `user = {}` would throw a TypeError. The object it points to is still mutable, so changing `user.name` works and logs "Bia". Nothing is ignored and there is no syntax error; to make the object itself read-only you would need something like Object.freeze.

title: var vs let inside an if block
options: It logs "admin" and then 10, since var and let are both visible
It throws a ReferenceError on `role`, before logging anything
It logs undefined, then throws a ReferenceError on `level`
It logs undefined twice, since both are hoisted to the function
explanation: `var` is function-scoped: `role` exists in the whole function and is hoisted with the value undefined, and since the if block never runs it stays undefined. `let` is block-scoped: `level` only exists inside the if block, so reading it outside throws "ReferenceError: level is not defined". Nothing inside the block runs with `false`, so "admin" and 10 are never assigned.

title: Returning an object from an arrow function
options: The braces are read as a function body, so nothing is returned
map skips the return value of arrows with a `name` parameter
An object literal cannot use the same name for key and value
Arrow functions cannot return objects, so use a regular function
explanation: After `=>`, a `{` starts a block body, not an object literal: `name:` is parsed as a label and `name` as an expression statement, and a block body without `return` returns undefined. Wrapping the literal in parentheses fixes it: `name => ({ name })`. Arrow functions can return objects this way, map uses every return value, and `{ name: name }` is a valid object literal.

title: Passing a function vs calling it
question:
`save` runs once when the page loads and then never again when the button is clicked. Why?

button.addEventListener("click", save());
options: addEventListener runs a listener once unless `{ once: false }` is set
The event name must be "onclick", so clicks are never matched
`save` must be declared after the button in the HTML file
`save()` runs it right away and passes its return value instead
explanation: The parentheses call `save` immediately while the listener is being registered, and its return value (usually undefined) is what gets passed to addEventListener, so no function is attached to the click. Pass the function itself: `addEventListener("click", save)`. Listeners run on every event by default, the event name is "click" ("onclick" is the property and attribute name), and declaration order in the HTML is not the issue.

title: Spread makes a shallow copy
options: Bia Natal
Ana Recife
Ana Natal
Bia Recife
explanation: Object spread makes a shallow copy: `copy` gets its own `name` property, so changing it leaves `original.name` as "Ana", but `copy.address` holds a reference to the same nested object as `original.address`. Changing the city through the copy therefore changes the original too. Copy the nested object as well (`{ ...original, address: { ...original.address } }`) or use structuredClone for a deep copy.

title: Forgetting await on an async function
options: "Ana", since the function does no real asynchronous work
undefined, because `user` is a Promise, not the object
It throws a TypeError, because `user` is still null
It waits for getUser to finish, and then logs "Ana"
explanation: An async function always returns a Promise, even when it returns a plain value without awaiting anything. `user` is that Promise, and a Promise has no `name` property, so the log is undefined. Nothing waits unless you use `await getUser()` (or `.then`), and `user` is never null, so no TypeError is thrown.

title: Independent awaits run one after another
options: About 1 s already, since `await` runs both requests in parallel
About 2 s; wrapping each `await` in try/catch runs them in parallel
About 1 s; Promise.all would only make the code shorter, not faster
About 2 s; use `await Promise.all([getOrders(), getInvoices()])`
explanation: Each `await` pauses until its promise settles, and getInvoices() is not even called until getOrders() has finished, so the total is about 2 s. Calling both first and awaiting `Promise.all` lets the two requests run at the same time, so the total is about the slower one, about 1 s. try/catch only handles errors and does not change timing.

title: querySelector returns null from a script in head
options: Add `defer` to the script tag, so it runs after the HTML is parsed
Use the selector `.save` instead, since querySelector cannot find ids
Attach the listener to `window`, since buttons cannot have one
Move the script tag above `<head>`, so it loads even earlier
explanation: A classic script in `<head>` runs as soon as it is reached, before the browser has parsed the body, so querySelector finds no `#save` element and returns null. `defer` (or placing the script at the end of the body) runs it after the document is parsed. `#save` is a valid id selector, buttons accept listeners, and loading the script even earlier makes the problem worse.

title: Inline onclick cannot see module functions
question: A page loads `<script type="module" src="app.js"></script>`. app.js declares `function handleClick() { ... }` at the top level, and the HTML has `<button onclick="handleClick()">Save</button>`. Clicking throws "ReferenceError: handleClick is not defined". Why?
options: Strict mode, which modules use, forbids top-level function declarations
Inline handlers can call arrow functions only, not function declarations
Top-level declarations in a module are module-scoped, not global
The `onclick` attribute needs `this.handleClick()` to reach module code
explanation: Each module has its own scope: its top-level declarations do not become globals or properties of `window`, unlike in a classic script. An inline `onclick` attribute looks names up in the global scope, so it cannot find handleClick. Attach the listener from the module with addEventListener (or, as a stopgap, assign `window.handleClick = handleClick`). Strict mode allows top-level function declarations, and inline handlers can call any global function.

title: try/catch around a promise that is not awaited
options: A catch block handles errors from `throw` only, never rejections
saveDraft() is not awaited, so its rejection never throws in the try
showToast runs first and clears the error before catch can see it
An async function cannot use try/catch, so `.catch()` is required
explanation: A rejected promise only becomes a thrown error where it is awaited. Without `await`, saveDraft() just returns a promise, the try block finishes normally and shows "Saved", and the rejection later has no handler, so it is reported as unhandled. Writing `await saveDraft();` makes the rejection throw inside the try, so catch runs. try/catch does catch awaited rejections, including inside async functions, and showToast has no effect on the error.
